On the $ZEC Dev Fund debate:

The Zcash community has decided its identity is “encrypted Bitcoin.” It has rejected adding more bells and whistles to the protocol. To become encrypted Bitcoin, Zcash must become a dependable store of value, and that means eventually ossifying.

But the protocol cannot ossify now. Tachyon and quantum-resistance will take work. AI cyber hardening eventually requires full formal verification. There’s a final version of Zcash that will be ready to ossify. But it’s hard to imagine that happening within the next year or two.

The Dev Fund has done a great job and was a necessary step to protect Zcash development at a time when there was no private funding for it. But there's a reason why the Dev Fund was not set to exist in perpetuity; under current rules it expires in 2028. But Zcash has run up so explosively, the size of that fund is an order of magnitude larger.

I'm sympathetic to @maxdesalle's argument that Zcash does not want to become like a government. The political economy of slush funds and “grantmaking” is genuinely corrupting. The sheer size of the Dev Fund, given how much Zcash has run up, has changed it. A few million dollars of funding can be thoughtfully allocated by a few individuals, but once you’re $100M+, you must become an institution. Zcash’s Dev Fund is now precisely in that no man’s land that it will not be able to avoid becoming politicized. I think you just have to accept that, and minimize it as best you can.

I believe the fund has to exist, at least for now. There's too much work left to do for a deeply technical project. But who governs that fund is a separate question.

I agree with @matthuang that pure tokenholder governance is too volatile for a store of value asset. American citizens don't get to vote on the Fed Funds rate at the ballot box, and Bitcoin holders don't vote on code changes. Predictability is a prerequisite for storing value. Institutions can be wasteful and distasteful, but they are predictable.

I’m of the opinion that this should be the final Dev Fund. It's large enough to fund the remaining work until Zcash is ready to ossify, and then wind down rather than search for other things to fund. If other work must be done afterward, it can be formed organically by holders and allies, just as it is for Bitcoin. I don’t think it should move toward pure tokenholder voting, though I’d be supportive of something partial. Councils suck, but they are often the best answer to a messy question.

(Normally I don’t weigh in on Zcash governance, but @zooko asked me to share my perspective. Take it with a grain of salt.)

Disclosure: Dragonfly holds $ZEC and I'm a personal investor in ZODL. ZODL does not benefit from the Dev Fund directly, but you should know where my incentives sit.

Hedge funds have become a major driver of the US Treasury market.

Hedge fund cash Treasury holdings stood at $2.35 trillion in Q1 2026, the 3rd-highest reading on record.

Over the last 5 years, this figure has surged +154%, or +$1.42 trillion.

For perspective, marketable Treasury debt outstanding increased +44% over the same period, to a record $32.2 trillion.

As a result, hedge funds now own a record ~7% of the marketable Treasury market, up from ~4% in 2021.

A major driver behind the surge is the cash-futures basis trade, where hedge funds take offsetting positions in Treasury securities and futures to profit from small price differences.

Because these gains are small, the strategy involves significant leverage.

This leverage allows hedge funds to absorb more Treasury debt at a time when the banks that normally help absorb new Treasury supply have limited capacity to hold more bonds.

Hedge funds are changing how the Treasury market works.

Not sure how people are bearish on memory....

On a side note was surprised markets from $AMD to $INTC rallied today after rate hikes. Think high-beta overshot the selloff the most.

Less than 2 years ago we still had a deeply anti-crypto SEC, led by Gary Gensler. And honestly, "anti-crypto SEC" doesn't even begin to describe it. It was an arbitrary witch hunt on our entire industry, one they seemed determined to destroy for whatever reasons they could find.

and hell yes did we stay.

Fast forward to today. We didn't just avert the danger and prove to the world that we're more than token rugpulls and useless whitepaper ICOs. We now have some of the most scalable and profitable businesses and use cases onchain, and the world is watching, being impressed.

At the same time, the most powerful institutions of the most powerful country in the world are now proactively embracing our industry, as this is what institutions want. What was harassed just 2 years ago is today being legalized, and actively encouraged, because they finally understood that if you want to keep your capital markets competitive, they have to be digitized.

and there's no better way to do that than with crypto rails.

so proud and grateful for everyone who fought for this and never let our industry go. today marks a historical milestone in disrupting the entire financial world, and I think the impact of this is beyond what most can imagine, as it unfolds over the coming months.

we made it.

3443 TT, Global Unichip limit up again, ATH.

We originally found GUC through Bitcoin. It was a major ASIC design partner for Bitcoin miners, which led us to research its unusually close relationship with TSMC and deep engineering bench.

Today that same capability is being monetized by AI. GUC is working on custom chips for Google, Tesla and other hyperscalers. August sales +111% YoY, driving today's action.

The contrast with Bitcoin mining machine makers is striking. CAN was in NY this week on an NDR. Despite having a competitive next-gen A16 miner ready, it has decided not to mass produce it. AI is soaking up advanced wafer capacity and pushing the economics against Bitcoin ASICs.

AI crowding out Bitcoin mining has reached the chip level.

The implications for Bitcoin are less obvious. Canaan’s retreat could mean still more dominance for Bitmain, with Bitdeer emerging as a credible challenger. But slower ASIC efficiency gains also mean existing machines become obsolete more slowly, reducing the reinvestment required to stay competitive. And to the extent hashrate growth slows or reverses, difficulty adjusts lower, providing yet another tailwind to margins for the miners who remain. Still, hard to frame hashrate decline a positive net net.

I agree with this and I keep trying every few months.

My killer app is having a casual info lookup / research tool that's >50% as good as internet + frontier models that can function on a fully offline phone.

(As people travel with their phones to situations where they're offline all the time)

There the goal is not even just CROPS, it's utility - and the problem is that if you're literally offline, magic remote FHE inference won't help you.

And so far I've gotten like 10 TPS with 1B models that break if you try to use them for anything interesting :(

I think the right architecture for phone might be extreme MoE (including newer varieties like ngrams), eg. you want like 100B params most of which live on disk and only <1B get activated per token

All this fear around AI taking your job misses a huge part of the story...

Labour force participation was falling long before AI showed up because it follows the birth rate with a twenty year lag, and birth rates have been falling for decades. 

So machines are mostly filling the gap left by people retiring or leaving the workforce anyway. That's a very different picture from the one you're being sold.

The old GDP equation ran on population growth plus productivity growth... synthetic labour removes that ceiling entirely. Productivity keeps compounding without needing more people to do it. 

That's the Economic Singularity, and it changes the whole equation.

by over-rotating on your positions trying to catch the latest thing, or worst still, chase what is pumping, you mathematically erode your gains

→ Y cools off and drops 27% from the top. you're now at $8k
→ meanwhile X, the token you sold, finally runs 50%

if you had done nothing: $15k
because you "did something": $8k. 7k gap from one rotation, and a +25% to get back to where you started

in a bull market, the most important thing to do, is sit on your hands. ideally you should have planned, allocated, and all you have left to do now

is to hold.

This is excellent. So much of agentic work is actually classification: routing to the right path, choosing the next action, or triaging context.

Imagine an email agent with 500 new emails but room for only 20 in its context window. Before any real reasoning begins, it needs to identify messages from important people, active projects, or urgent threads.

For each email, Jev could return something directly usable by code:

include_in_context: true
category: active_project
urgency: 0.91
confidence: 0.97

Jev could be a game changer for latency and cost. Instead of generating an answer token by token, it returns typed decisions and probabilities in parallel.

And it’s much more versatile than training a traditional BERT-style classifier for every task. You keep the flexibility of a prompt + runtime context, with the speed and predictable output of a classifier. Basically the programmability of a language model shaped like a classifier so it’s very cool. Congrats @CompleteSkeptic, you cooked!
